newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa forecasts may crystallize with new arrivals.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa forecasts may crystallize with new arrivals.

text.p: Ivory Coast cocoa arrivals this month will be closely monitored by analysts who are trying to decide whether dry weather there means that forecasts for abundant supply this year need any revision.
Crop experts have said that output from the world's largest grower may be just short of last year's record but the outlook is now somewhat blurred by a prolonged dry spell.
The West African dry season normally begins in November but pod counters scouting the Ivorian cocoa fields reported unusually low levels of soil moisture at the end of October.
Early drought affects the survival of the tail of the crop, usually the last 100,000 tonnes, and may reduce the bean size.
But forecasters, caught off guard last year by the late shaping of the bumper crop, are reluctant to modify scenarios that envisaged abundant supply this year until they gather more evidence.

"It's not going to make a huge difference for the overall total of the crop because your setting at that time is pretty light anyway," said Robert Fish of UK forecaster PCR Ltd. "We won't really know until we get arrivals figures until the end of this month because we're all trying to forecast the last counts when stuff had already been taken off the trees. Although arrivals got off to a slow start after delays in export licences and problems in financing -- estimates by November 2 are between 120,000-125,000 tonnes from 135,000 last year -- the crop itself is not behind schedule.

As a rule of thumb, arrivals of 250,000 tonnes by the end of November will confirm a main crop in excess of 900,000 tonnes and a likely total around 1.05 million compared with 1.2 million in the 1995/96 season (Oct-Sept), forecasters said.
In Ghana, crop analysts are looking for a main harvest of about 310,000 tonnes, some 45,000 down on last year.

London cocoa futures have fallen 15 percent since August as the big crop estimates knocked sentiment just as the market was reeling under last year's surplus. A rigid downtrend channel has formed over the charts, suggesting further price drops.
March cocoa was nearly at eight-month lows on Tuesday when it traded at 908 stg a tonne.
Cocoa consumption is increasing but analysts expect a net rise in stocks between the 1995/96 and 1996/97 seasons.
"I don't think the main crop people are worried at the moment," said a Swiss-based physical trader.

For the most part, chocolate manufacturers are covered for the first quarter of 1997 and in no rush to make forward purchases. But they could begin to refill stocks for the summer if talk of damage from the dry spell is justified, traders said.

"Nobody wants to be caught with the small bean cocoa. Especially with the carry at the moment it would pay off to buy fresh shipments at the height of the main crop season and just carry it through the season," said the Swiss trader.
Brokers Merrill Lynch said the downside in prices was likely to be limited for now, but pressure could be restored if production prospects improved dramatically in the new year.

"We still believe that production figures are more apt to be revised upwards later in the year than lower and this prevents us from being friendly towards the market at these lower levels," Merrill Lynch said in a monthly commentary.
